```{r prep}
#| include: false
# All results are read from the files in results/category-fit/. The
# simulations are in scripts/category-fit/ (see @sec-cfit-reproduction).
RES <- "results/category-fit"
s <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "summary.rds"))
alpha <- s$alpha
d <- as.data.frame(s$reps) |>
  mutate(evaluable = is.na(skipped) & !is.na(B_used) & B_used > 0,
         cell = sprintf("n = %d, k = %d", n, k))
ok <- filter(d, evaluable)

cal <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "calibration_summary.rds"))$reps |>
  mutate(evaluable = is.na(skipped) & !is.na(B_used) & B_used > 0,
         cell = sprintf("n = %d, k = %d", n, k))
cal_ok <- filter(cal, evaluable)
# Item p (studentised max-T over the events) and its Westfall-Young
# step-down, for every item of every dataset.
cal_items <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "compare_combination.rds"))$items |>
  transmute(cond, null, n, k, rep, item, p = p_max, padj = padj_max)
b999 <- readRDS(file.path(RES, "calibration_b999_summary.rds"))$strict

cond_labels <- c(
  A0_pcm_ordered    = "PCM, ordered",
  A1_pcm_disordered = "PCM, disordered",
  S_outer_a0        = "Categories 0, 1 interchangeable",
  S_inner_a0        = "Categories 1, 2 interchangeable",
  S_inner_a05       = "Step 2 discrimination .5",
  S_inner_a2        = "Step 2 discrimination 2",
  SWAP_1_2          = "Categories 1, 2 swapped",
  DK_wide_05        = "Don't know 5%, wide middle",
  DK_wide_10        = "Don't know 10%, wide middle",
  DK_wide_25        = "Don't know 25%, wide middle",
  DK_narrow_05      = "Don't know 5%, narrow middle",
  DK_narrow_10      = "Don't know 10%, narrow middle",
  DK_narrow_25      = "Don't know 25%, narrow middle",
  ERS_30            = "Extreme response style 30%")
lab <- function(x) factor(cond_labels[as.character(x)], levels = cond_labels)

# Per-category statistics: Okabe-Ito, validated for four nominal series
# (all-pairs CVD dE 11.0). Every series also has its own shape and line type.
pal_stat <- c(Mean = "#0072B2", SD = "#D55E00", Q = "#009E73", Tail = "#56B4E9")
scale_stat <- list(
  scale_colour_manual("Statistic", values = pal_stat),
  scale_shape_manual("Statistic", values = c(Mean = 16, SD = 17, Q = 15, Tail = 1)),
  scale_linetype_manual("Statistic", values = c(Mean = "solid", SD = "42",
                                                Q = "dotdash", Tail = "dotted")))
theme_set(theme_book(base_size = 10) +
            theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.spacing = unit(0.4, "cm")))

stat_long <- ok |>
  select(cond, null, n, k, cell, rep, matches("^p_(mean|sd|tail|Q)_\\d$")) |>
  pivot_longer(matches("^p_"), names_to = c("stat", "category"),
               names_pattern = "p_(mean|sd|tail|Q)_(\\d)", values_to = "p") |>
  mutate(stat = factor(c(mean = "Mean", sd = "SD", tail = "Tail", Q = "Q")[stat],
                       levels = names(pal_stat)),
         category = as.integer(category))
rej <- stat_long |>
  group_by(cond, null, n, k, cell, stat, category) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(p < alpha), reps = n(), .groups = "drop")
idx <- ok |>
  group_by(cond, null, n, k) |>
  summarise(index = mean(p_index1 < alpha), wald = mean(disorder_any),
            disordered = mean(disorder_pt), .groups = "drop")

# Calibration test
null_cell <- cal_items |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(r01 = mean(p < .01), r05 = mean(p < alpha), min_p = min(p),
            .groups = "drop")
null_all <- cal_items |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(k) |>
  summarise(r05 = mean(p < alpha), .groups = "drop")
fwer <- cal_items |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k, rep) |>
  summarise(any = any(padj < alpha), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(datasets = n(), fw = mean(any), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(.05 * .95 / datasets))
fw_top <- slice_max(fwer, fw, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
event_null <- cal_ok |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(paste0("p_raw_", 1:4)), ~ mean(.x < alpha)),
            .groups = "drop")
pow <- bind_rows(
  cal_items |> filter(!null, item == 1) |> group_by(cond, n, k) |>
    summarise(rate = mean(p < alpha), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(test = "Calibration test"),
  ok |> filter(!null) |> group_by(cond, n, k) |>
    summarise(rate = mean(p_index1 < alpha), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(test = "Item index"))
pow_big <- pow |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = test, values_from = rate) |>
  mutate(d = `Calibration test` - `Item index`) |>
  filter(pmax(`Calibration test`, `Item index`) > .2)
pow_adj <- cal_items |>
  filter(!null, item == 1) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(adj = mean(padj < alpha), .groups = "drop")
kept <- pow |>
  filter(test == "Calibration test") |>
  select(cond, n, k, before = rate) |>
  inner_join(pow_adj, by = c("cond", "n", "k")) |>
  filter(before > .2) |>
  mutate(share = adj / before,
         scale = cond %in% c("SWAP_1_2", "S_outer_a0", "S_inner_a0"))
other_adj <- cal_items |>
  filter(!null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k, rep) |>
  summarise(any_other = any(padj[item > 1] < alpha), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(any_other), .groups = "drop")

# Inline helpers
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
rng <- function(x, f = pct) paste(f(min(x)), "to", f(max(x)))
f3 <- function(x) sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", x))
f2 <- function(x) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", sprintf("%.2f", x))
rr <- function(cnd, st, ct) rej$rate[rej$cond == cnd & rej$stat == st & rej$category == ct]
pw <- function(cnd, nn, kk, tst = "Calibration test") {
  pct(pow$rate[pow$cond == cnd & pow$n == nn & pow$k == kk & pow$test == tst])
}
pw_rng <- function(cnd, tst = "Calibration test") rng(pow$rate[pow$cond == cnd & pow$test == tst])
pa <- function(cnd, nn, kk) pct(pow_adj$adj[pow_adj$cond == cnd & pow_adj$n == nn & pow_adj$k == kk])
pa_rng <- function(cnd) rng(pow_adj$adj[pow_adj$cond == cnd])
b9 <- function(cnd, col) b999[[col]][b999$cond == cnd]
```

## Summary

Disordered threshold estimates are often read as a sign that a response scale
does not work, but the partial credit model (PCM) allows any threshold order.
This chapter asks a different question: do the categories of an item work as
the scoring 0, 1, ..., m says? Given a respondent's total score, the PCM
predicts the probability of each category from the item parameters alone, so
the observed responses can be compared with the model without estimating any
person location. `RMitemCatFit()` turns this into one test per item. It
compares the observed share of responses at or above each category with the
predicted probability, and simulates the reference distribution given the
observed total scores. When the PCM held, the item p-value rejected in
`r rng(null_cell$r05, f3)` of items per condition at .05, and with the
correction across items, at least one item was flagged in
`r rng(fwer$fw, f3)` of datasets per condition. The test detected swapped
categories (`r pw_rng("SWAP_1_2")` of datasets) and interchangeable categories
(categories 0 and 1 in `r pw_rng("S_outer_a0")`, categories 1 and 2 in
`r pw_rng("S_inner_a0")`), all with ordered threshold estimates, which a Wald
test of threshold order flagged in at most
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * max(idx$wald[idx$cond %in% c("SWAP_1_2", "S_outer_a0", "S_inner_a0")]))`
of these datasets. With disordered thresholds and the PCM true, the Wald test
flagged `r rng(idx$wald[idx$cond == "A1_pcm_disordered"])` of datasets and
`RMitemCatFit()` close to its nominal rate. `RMitemCatFitPlot()` shows
where an item departs, and the event that departs points to the step
concerned.
:::

## Purpose {#sec-cfit-purpose}

The categories of a polytomous item are scored 0, 1, ..., m and the scores
are added. That scoring assumes that each category is a step up from the one
below. Several things can make it wrong: two categories that respondents do
not distinguish since category labels are too similar or nonexisting, a step
that separates respondents much more or less than the others, or a neutral Likert-style middle
category used as "don't know".

Ordered response category thresholds are one of the basic psychometric
criteria summarised by @christensen2021, and disordered threshold estimates
are commonly taken as the signal that a response scale does not work as intended. The debate about
what disordered thresholds mean is unresolved [@andrichExpandedDerivationThreshold2013;@adamsRaschRatingModel2012;@garciaperezAnalysisDisOrderedCategories2017;@wetzelReversedThresholdsPartial2014;@anselmiAssessingThresholdOrdering2026]. The PCM itself allows any threshold order, so a disordered
estimate is not a departure from the model. And a scale can fail in the ways
listed above with ordered thresholds. This chapter studies a test of the
scoring that does not depend on the threshold order, and plots that show
where an item departs. Both are in easyRasch2: `RMitemCatFit()` for the test
and `RMitemCatFitPlot()` for the plots.

## Background {#sec-cfit-background}

### Category probabilities given the total score {#sec-cfit-conditional}

Under the PCM the total score $r$ is sufficient for the person location. Given
$r$, the probability that a respondent chose category $j$ of item $i$ depends
only on the item parameters:

$$P(X_i = j \mid r) = \frac{\varepsilon_{ij}\,\gamma^{(i)}_{r-j}}{\gamma_r},$$

where $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is the category parameter and $\gamma_r$ and
$\gamma^{(i)}_{r-j}$ are elementary symmetric functions of all items and of
all items except $i$. The table of items and categories by total score
therefore has expected counts that involve no person parameters. This table
is the basis of Glas's tests for the Rasch model [@glas1988] and the PCM
[@glas1989]. The item parameters are estimated by conditional maximum
likelihood (CML), so the comparison is not affected by error in person
estimates.

Summed over the total scores, the expected count of each category equals the
observed count, because the category counts are sufficient for the CML
estimates. A plain comparison of observed and expected category frequencies
therefore shows nothing. Differences appear only when respondents are split
by total score, which both the test and the plots do.

### Cumulative events and calibration {#sec-cfit-calibration}

For each item and each category $k \ge 1$, the event $X_i \ge k$ has the
predicted probability $p = P(X_i \ge k \mid r)$. If the categories work as
scored, the observed share of respondents with $X_i \ge k$ follows $p$ across
the score range. If two categories are not distinguished or are used in the
wrong order, the event at the step between them depends less on the total
score than predicted.

The observed events are compared with $p$ by the pool-adjacent-violators
(PAV) algorithm, which gives the best non-decreasing fit of the observed
events to $p$, the conditional event probability (CEP). A plot of the CEP
against $p$ is a PAV-adjusted reliability diagram [@dimitriadis2021], the
calibration plot recommended for ordinal outcomes by @sailynoja2025. Here
the prediction comes from the total score instead of a person estimate.
Because CML reproduces each category's count, the curve cannot lie above or
below the diagonal overall. It can only cross it. A curve flatter than the
diagonal means that the event separates respondents less well than predicted,
and a steeper one that it separates them better.

### The test {#sec-cfit-test}

The statistic for each event is the miscalibration component of the Brier
score in the CORP decomposition [@dimitriadis2021]:

$$\text{MCB} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_v (p_v - y_v)^2 - \frac{1}{n}\sum_v (\hat c_v - y_v)^2,$$

where $y_v$ is 1 when respondent $v$ scored $k$ or higher and $\hat c_v$ is
the CEP. MCB is zero when the curve lies on the diagonal and grows with its
distance from it. Respondents with the lowest or highest possible total score
are left out, since their responses are fixed by the score.

The reference distribution is simulated given each respondent's observed total
score. Response patterns are drawn from $P(\mathbf{x} \mid r)$ at the CML
estimates, so no person location is drawn, and the item parameters are
re-estimated in every simulated dataset. The fit of the prediction to the
same data is therefore part of the reference distribution. Simulated datasets
with an empty category in some item cannot be refitted and are dropped.

For each event, p is the share of the observed MCB and the $B$ simulated ones
that lie at or above the observed value. The events of an item are combined
by a studentised maximum: each event's MCB is centred and scaled by the mean
and SD of the observed and simulated values together, and the item statistic
is the largest of the item's values. The item p is the share of the observed
and simulated item statistics at or above the observed one, so the smallest
attainable p is $1/(B + 1)$. Across items, the Westfall-Young step-down on the
item statistics gives p-values corrected for the family-wise error rate
[@ge2003]. `RMitemCatFit()` uses this correction by default and offers the
false discovery rate corrections of @benjamini1995 as alternatives.

## Using the functions {#sec-cfit-example}

```{r example-data}
#| include: false
# Generators from the simulation study (scripts/category-fit/study_functions.R).
source("scripts/category-fit/study_functions.R")
set.seed(2026)
n_ex <- 1000
theta <- stats::rnorm(n_ex)
q1 <- sim_steps(theta, WIDE)
q1 <- c(0L, 2L, 1L, 3L, 4L)[q1 + 1L]              # categories 1 and 2 swapped
q2 <- sim_steps(theta, WIDE, c(0, 1, 1, 1))       # categories 0 and 1 interchangeable
ex <- as.data.frame(cbind(q1, q2, sim_pcm(theta, other_items(7))))
names(ex) <- paste0("Q", seq_len(ncol(ex)))
```

The example has `r n_ex` simulated respondents and `r ncol(ex)` items with
five categories (0 to 4). Items Q3 to Q8 follow the PCM. Q1 follows the PCM
with ordered thresholds, but categories 1 and 2 are swapped, as when the
second and third response options are in the wrong order. In Q2, categories
0 and 1 are interchangeable: the first step does not depend on the person
location.

```{r example-thresholds}
#| include: false
thr_ex <- easyRasch2:::.fit_cml_thresholds(ex)
thr_txt <- function(it) paste(sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", sprintf("%.2f", thr_ex[[it]])), collapse = ", ")
all_ordered <- all(vapply(thr_ex, function(t) !is.unsorted(t), logical(1L)))
```

The usual first look at the response categories is a plot of the category
probability curves against the person location (@fig-cfit-example-catprob).
In these data the threshold estimates of every item are
`r if (all_ordered) "ordered" else "not all ordered"`, Q1 at
(`r thr_txt("Q1")`) and Q2 at (`r thr_txt("Q2")`), and the curves of Q1 and
Q2 look like those of the PCM items. Nothing in this plot shows that two of
the items do not work as scored.

```{r fig-cfit-example-catprob}
#| label: fig-cfit-example-catprob
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Category probability curves of the example data, from RMitemCatProb(). The thresholds of every item, including Q1 and Q2, are estimated in order."
RMitemCatProb(ex)
```

```{r example-fit}
fit <- RMitemCatFit(ex, seed = 1, output = "list")
```

```{r example-numbers}
#| include: false
tb <- fit$table
cal_ex <- RMitemCatFitPlot(ex, type = "calibration", fit = fit, output = "dataframe")
out_share <- cal_ex |>
  mutate(out = cep < lower | cep > upper) |>
  group_by(item, event) |>
  summarise(share = mean(out), .groups = "drop")
os <- function(it, ev) pct(out_share$share[out_share$item == it & out_share$event == ev])
os_pcm <- out_share$share[!out_share$item %in% c("Q1", "Q2")]
res_ex <- RMitemCatFitPlot(ex, type = "residuals", output = "dataframe")
n_beyond <- tapply(abs(res_ex$z) > 1.96, res_ex$item, sum, na.rm = TRUE)
n_cells <- tapply(!is.na(res_ex$z), res_ex$item, sum)
rs_ex <- RMitemCatFitPlot(ex, type = "restscore", fit = fit, output = "dataframe")
rs_out <- with(rs_ex, tapply(observed < lower | observed > upper, item, sum, na.rm = TRUE))
# "< .001" or "= .027", for "p < .001" / "p = .027" in the text
pq <- function(it, col = "p") {
  v <- tb[[col]][tb$item == it]
  if (v < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", f3(v))
}
# Slope of the observed and expected share in the upper category against the
# total score, weighted by the respondents in the pair
adj_ex <- RMitemCatFitPlot(ex, type = "adjacent", output = "dataframe")
slope <- function(it, pr, col) {
  a <- adj_ex[adj_ex$item == it & adj_ex$pair == pr, ]
  unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(a[[col]] ~ a$score, weights = a$n_pair))[2])
}
q2_ratio <- slope("Q2", "1 vs 0", "observed") / slope("Q2", "1 vs 0", "expected")
```

The test table has one row per item with the p for each event, the item p and
the item p corrected across items (@tbl-cfit-example in the appendix). For
Q1 the item p is the smallest attainable with `r fit$iterations_used`
simulated datasets (p `r pq("Q1")`, corrected p `r pq("Q1", "padj")`), and
its event $X \ge 2$, the step between the swapped categories, has
p `r pq("Q1", "p_2")`. For Q2, p `r pq("Q2")` and corrected
p `r pq("Q2", "padj")`, with p `r pq("Q2", "p_1")` for $X \ge 1$, the step
between the interchangeable categories. For the PCM item Q3, p `r pq("Q3")`
and corrected p `r pq("Q3", "padj")`. With eight items, an item
p near .02 for some item is not unusual when the model holds, which is what
the correction accounts for. In these data the correction leaves Q2's
departure undetected as well.

The calibration plot (@fig-cfit-example-calibration) shows each item's
corrected p under its label when the result of `RMitemCatFit()` is passed as
`fit`, so the simulations are not repeated.

```{r fig-cfit-example-calibration}
#| label: fig-cfit-example-calibration
#| fig-height: 11
#| fig-cap: "Calibration plot of the example data, from RMitemCatFitPlot(type = \"calibration\", fit = fit). One row per item, one column per cumulative event. Under each item label: its p corrected across items."
RMitemCatFitPlot(ex, type = "calibration", fit = fit)
```

For Q1 the curve for $X \ge 2$ is much flatter than the diagonal, and
`r os("Q1", "X ≥ 2")` of its points lie outside the band. For Q2 it is the
curve for $X \ge 1$ that is flatter (`r os("Q2", "X ≥ 1")` of the points
outside). For the six PCM items, `r rng(os_pcm)` of the points per event lie
outside. The band is pointwise, so with many points some fall outside it when
the model holds, and the plot shows where to look rather than whether an item
fits.

```{r fig-cfit-example-residuals}
#| label: fig-cfit-example-residuals
#| fig-height: 11
#| fig-cap: "Standardised residuals of the category counts within five groups of total scores, from RMitemCatFitPlot(type = \"residuals\", fit = fit)."
RMitemCatFitPlot(ex, type = "residuals", fit = fit)
```

The residual plot (@fig-cfit-example-residuals) splits the respondents into
groups of total scores. For Q1, category 2 is chosen more often than expected
in the low score groups and category 1 in the high groups, with
`r n_beyond["Q1"]` of `r n_cells["Q1"]` residuals beyond ±1.96, against
`r rng(n_beyond[3:8], function(x) x)` per PCM item.

```{r fig-cfit-example-adjacent}
#| label: fig-cfit-example-adjacent
#| fig-height: 11
#| fig-cap: "Share of respondents in the upper of two adjacent categories at each total score, among respondents in either, from RMitemCatFitPlot(type = \"adjacent\", fit = fit). Line: expected under the PCM. Band: pointwise 95% binomial range."
RMitemCatFitPlot(ex, type = "adjacent", fit = fit)
```

Under the PCM, the share in the upper of two adjacent categories rises with
the total score (@fig-cfit-example-adjacent). For Q1 the share in category 2
among respondents in categories 1 or 2 falls instead. For Q2 the share in
category 1 among respondents in 0 or 1 rises with the score, but at about
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * q2_ratio)` of the expected slope.

```{r fig-cfit-example-restscore}
#| label: fig-cfit-example-restscore
#| fig-height: 11
#| fig-cap: "Rest-score mean and SD per category, observed minus expected, against the pointwise 95% range in the simulated datasets, from RMitemCatFitPlot(type = \"restscore\", fit = fit)."
RMitemCatFitPlot(ex, type = "restscore", fit = fit)
```

The rest-score plot (@fig-cfit-example-restscore) compares the rest score (total
score minus the item's score) of the respondents in each category with its
expected value. These are the statistics studied in @sec-cfit-categories. For
Q1, `r rs_out["Q1"]` of the 10 statistics lie outside their range. The
plot is most useful for "don't know" use, which shows as a wider spread of
the rest score in the middle category (@sec-cfit-categories).

## Simulation study {#sec-cfit-study}

### Design {#sec-cfit-design}

**Data.** $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$. One focus item (item 1) and $k - 1$ other
items, each with five categories scored 0 to 4. The other items follow the
PCM, with locations spread evenly over $[-1, 1]$, thresholds
$(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)$ around the location and a fixed jitter (SD 0.2).
Sample sizes n = 250, 500 and 1000, with k = 5 or 10 items.

**Conditions for the focus item** (location 0).

- *PCM, ordered:* thresholds $(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)$.
- *PCM, disordered:* thresholds $(-1.5, 0.4, -0.4, 1.5)$, in which the
  middle category is rare and never the most probable.
- *Step discriminations* [@glas1989, section 7]:
  $P(X = j \mid \theta) \propto \exp\{\sum_{l \le j} a_l(\theta - \delta_l)\}$
  with the ordered thresholds. $a_1 = 0$ makes categories 0 and 1
  interchangeable, $a_2 = 0$ makes 1 and 2 interchangeable, and
  $a_2 = 0.5$ or $2$ makes step 2 flatter or steeper than the scoring
  assumes.
- *Swapped categories:* responses generated under the ordered PCM, then
  categories 1 and 2 relabelled as each other.
- *"Don't know" use:* with probability .05, .10 or .25, the middle category
  is chosen whatever $\theta$, on the ordered (wide middle) or the
  disordered (narrow middle) thresholds.
- *Extreme response style:* 30% of respondents answer every item with
  thresholds compressed towards the item location (factor 0.3).

**Tests.** Two sets of tests used the same conditions on separate datasets.
The first is a set of per-category statistics, each tested against the same
simulated reference distribution as `RMitemCatFit()`: for each category $j$
of the focus item, the mean and SD of the rest score among respondents in
that category, the number of them with a total score in the lowest or
highest 10% (tail), each as observed minus expected, and $Q_j$, the sum over
score levels of the squared standardised deviations for that category. The
item index is the sum of $Q_j$ over $j \ge 1$. As comparisons, a Wald test of
threshold order flags an item when any adjacent pair of threshold estimates
is disordered with $z < -1.645$, using the CML covariance matrix. The second
is the calibration test of @sec-cfit-test, for every item.

**Replication.** Datasets with the PCM true: 500 per cell with $B = 199$.
Other conditions: 200 per cell with $B = 99$. The Monte Carlo SE of a rate of
.05 is .010 and .015. The condition with the highest family-wise rate was run
again with $B = 999$ and 1000 new datasets per cell. A dataset with an empty
category in the observed data was skipped, and one in which no simulated
dataset could be refitted was left out of the rates (@tbl-cfit-evaluable).

### Threshold order {#sec-cfit-order}

With the PCM true and ordered thresholds, the Wald test never flagged
disorder. With the disordered thresholds, which the PCM fits, it flagged
`r rng(idx$wald[idx$cond == "A1_pcm_disordered"])` of datasets. In the
conditions in which the scale does not work as scored, the estimates stayed
ordered. With categories 1 and 2 swapped, the mean threshold estimates of
steps 2 and 3 at n = 1000 and k = 10 were
`r f2(mean(ok$t2[ok$cond == "SWAP_1_2" & ok$n == 1000 & ok$k == 10]))` and
`r f2(mean(ok$t3[ok$cond == "SWAP_1_2" & ok$n == 1000 & ok$k == 10]))`,
ordered but close (@tbl-cfit-thresholds). For swapped and interchangeable
categories, the Wald test flagged at most
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * max(idx$wald[idx$cond %in% c("SWAP_1_2", "S_outer_a0", "S_inner_a0")]))`
of datasets. "Don't know" use at 10% or 25% on the narrow middle removed the
disorder: the Wald test then flagged at most
`r pct(max(idx$wald[idx$cond %in% c("DK_narrow_10", "DK_narrow_25")]))`. In
these data, disordered threshold estimates were neither necessary nor
sufficient for a response scale that does not work as scored.

### Per-category statistics {#sec-cfit-categories}

```{r fig-cfit-cat-null}
#| label: fig-cfit-cat-null
#| fig-height: 7.5
#| fig-cap: "Rejection rate at .05 of each per-category statistic when the PCM holds, by condition and number of items (rows) and sample size (columns). The grey band is .05 plus or minus two Monte Carlo SEs."
rej |>
  filter(null) |>
  mutate(row = paste0(lab(cond), ", k = ", k)) |>
  ggplot(aes(category, rate, colour = stat, shape = stat, linetype = stat)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = .05 - 2 * .0097,
           ymax = .05 + 2 * .0097, fill = "grey85") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_grid(row ~ factor(paste("n =", n), levels = paste("n =", c(250, 500, 1000)))) +
  scale_stat +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, .1)) +
  labs(x = "Category of the focus item", y = "Rejection rate") +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(size = 7))
```

With the PCM true, each of the 20 per-category statistics and the item index
rejected in `r rng(c(rej$rate[rej$null], idx$index[idx$null]), f3)` of
datasets per cell, a little under .05 on average (@fig-cfit-cat-null). The
same held with disordered thresholds.

```{r fig-cfit-cat-power}
#| label: fig-cfit-cat-power
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Rejection rate at .05 of each per-category statistic at n = 500 and k = 10, by condition. Dotted line at .05."
rej |>
  filter(!null, n == 500, k == 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(category, rate, colour = stat, shape = stat, linetype = stat)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab(cond), ncol = 3) +
  scale_stat +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Category of the focus item", y = "Rejection rate") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 7.5))
```

Each kind of departure showed in a particular statistic
(@fig-cfit-cat-power).

- **Swapped categories.** The rest-score means of categories 1 and 2
  rejected in every dataset at every sample size.
- **Interchangeable categories.** With categories 1 and 2 interchangeable, the
  category 1 mean rejected in `r rng(rr("S_inner_a0", "Mean", 1))` of
  datasets. With categories 0 and 1 interchangeable, $Q_0$ and the category 1
  mean rejected in `r rng(c(rr("S_outer_a0", "Q", 0), rr("S_outer_a0", "Mean", 1)))`.
- **Step discriminations.** A step 2 that discriminated twice as strongly or
  half as strongly showed mainly in the category means.
- **"Don't know" use** showed as a wider spread of the middle category, not
  as a shifted mean. At 25%, the SD of category 2 rejected in
  `r rng(rr("DK_wide_25", "SD", 2))` of datasets with the wide middle and
  `r rng(rr("DK_narrow_25", "SD", 2))` with the narrow middle. At 5%, it
  rejected in `r rng(c(rr("DK_wide_05", "SD", 2), rr("DK_narrow_05", "SD", 2)))`.
- **An extreme response style shared by all items** was not detected
  (`r rng(c(rej$rate[rej$cond == "ERS_30"], idx$index[idx$cond == "ERS_30"]))`
  for every statistic). The test compares the focus item with the other
  items, and a style that affects every item alike leaves that comparison
  unchanged.

The item index, the sum of the $Q_j$, was weak for several of these
departures: `r rng(idx$index[idx$cond == "S_outer_a0"])` for categories 0 and
1 interchangeable and `r rng(idx$index[idx$cond == "S_inner_a2"])` for a step
that discriminated twice as strongly (@tbl-cfit-calibration). Each
per-category statistic is calibrated on its own, but a reader who looks at
all 20 and acts on any p < .05 would reject in about half of the datasets
when the PCM holds. The per-category statistics therefore describe a
departure once it is found, which is how `RMitemCatFitPlot(type = "restscore")`
shows them, and the calibration test serves as the single test per item.

### The calibration test when the PCM holds {#sec-cfit-cal-null}

```{r fig-cfit-cal-null}
#| label: fig-cfit-cal-null
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Share of item p-values at or below α when the PCM holds, over all items of every dataset, by condition (rows), sample size (columns) and number of items. Points at α = .01, .025, .05 and .10. Dotted diagonal: a calibrated p-value. B = 199."
a_grid <- seq(0, .1, by = .0025)
pal_k <- c("k = 5" = "#0072B2", "k = 10" = "#D55E00")
cal_items |>
  filter(null) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  reframe(a = a_grid, rate = ecdf(p)(a_grid)) |>
  mutate(k = factor(paste("k =", k), levels = names(pal_k)),
         n = factor(paste("n =", n), levels = paste("n =", c(250, 500, 1000)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(a, rate, colour = k, linetype = k, shape = k)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_step() +
  geom_point(data = \(d) filter(d, round(a, 4) %in% c(.01, .025, .05, .1)),
             size = 2) +
  facet_grid(lab(cond) ~ n) +
  scale_colour_manual("Items", values = pal_k) +
  scale_linetype_manual("Items", values = c("solid", "42")) +
  scale_shape_manual("Items", values = c(16, 17)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, .05, .1), labels = c("0", ".05", ".10")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, .05, .1), labels = c("0", ".05", ".10")) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, .1), ylim = c(0, .1)) +
  labs(x = "α", y = "Share of p ≤ α")
```

The item p was close to uniform in its lower tail (@fig-cfit-cal-null). Over
all items it rejected at .05 in `r f3(null_all$r05[null_all$k == 5])` of
items at k = 5 and `r f3(null_all$r05[null_all$k == 10])` at k = 10, between
`r f3(min(null_cell$r05))` and `r f3(max(null_cell$r05))` per cell, and at
.01 between `r f3(min(null_cell$r01))` and `r f3(max(null_cell$r01))` per
cell. At B = 199 the item p rejects slightly less often than nominal at .01,
because only a few p-values below .01 are attainable. The p of each single
event rejected at .05 in
`r rng(unlist(event_null[, paste0("p_raw_", 1:4)]), f3)` of datasets per
cell.

With the correction across items, at least one item was flagged in
`r rng(fwer$fw, f3)` of datasets per cell (@tbl-cfit-cal-null). The highest
rate, `r f3(fw_top$fw)`, was in the `r as.character(lab(fw_top$cond))`
condition at n = `r fw_top$n` and k = `r fw_top$k`, and every other cell was
at or below `r f3(sort(fwer$fw, decreasing = TRUE)[2])`. With $B = 999$ and
`r b999$datasets[1]` new datasets, the family-wise rate at n = 1000 and
k = 5 was `r f3(b9("A0_pcm_ordered", "fwer"))` with ordered and
`r f3(b9("A1_pcm_disordered", "fwer"))` with disordered thresholds (Monte
Carlo SE `r f3(b999$se[1])`), and the item p rejected at .05 in
`r f3(b9("A0_pcm_ordered", "item_05"))` and
`r f3(b9("A1_pcm_disordered", "item_05"))` of items. The first 199 simulated
datasets of the same runs gave family-wise rates of
`r f3(b9("A0_pcm_ordered", "sub199_fwer"))` and
`r f3(b9("A1_pcm_disordered", "sub199_fwer"))`, so the smaller B did not
raise the rate, and the `r f3(fw_top$fw)` is most likely chance.

### Detection {#sec-cfit-cal-power}

```{r fig-cfit-cal-power}
#| label: fig-cfit-cal-power
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Rejection rate at .05 for the focus item of the calibration test (item p before the correction across items) and of the item index, by condition, sample size and number of items. The two tests were run on different datasets from the same conditions. Dotted line at .05."
pal_test <- c("Calibration test" = "#0072B2", "Item index" = "#D55E00")
pow |>
  mutate(test = paste0(test, ", k = ", k)) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, rate, colour = test, shape = test, linetype = test)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab(cond), ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual("Test", values = rep(pal_test, each = 2)) +
  scale_shape_manual("Test", values = c(16, 1, 17, 2)) +
  scale_linetype_manual("Test", values = c("solid", "42", "solid", "42")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(250, 500, 1000), trans = "log10",
                     expand = expansion(mult = .12)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Sample size", y = "Rejection rate") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 7.5),
        panel.spacing.x = unit(1.2, "lines"))
```

In every cell where either test rejected in more than 20% of datasets, the
calibration test rejected
`r if (min(pow_big$d) >= 0) "at least as often as the item index" else sprintf("about as often as the item index or more often, at most %.1f percentage points less", -100 * min(pow_big$d))`
(@fig-cfit-cal-power). The largest differences:

- Categories 0 and 1 interchangeable: `r pw_rng("S_outer_a0")` against
  `r pw_rng("S_outer_a0", "Item index")` for the item index.
- Step 2 discrimination 2: `r pw("S_inner_a2", 1000, 10)` against
  `r pw("S_inner_a2", 1000, 10, "Item index")` at n = 1000 and k = 10.
- Categories 1 and 2 interchangeable at k = 10: `r pw("S_inner_a0", 250, 10)`
  against `r pw("S_inner_a0", 250, 10, "Item index")` at n = 250.
- Categories 1 and 2 swapped at n = 250 and k = 10:
  `r pw("SWAP_1_2", 250, 10)` against `r pw("SWAP_1_2", 250, 10, "Item index")`.

Both tests rarely detected "don't know" use at 5 or 10% (at most
`r pct(max(pow$rate[pow$test == "Calibration test" & grepl("DK_(wide|narrow)_(05|10)", pow$cond)]))`
for the calibration test), and the calibration test did not detect the
extreme response style (`r pw_rng("ERS_30")`).

After the correction across the k items, the focus item was flagged in
`r pa_rng("SWAP_1_2")` of datasets with swapped categories,
`r pa_rng("S_outer_a0")` with categories 0 and 1 interchangeable and
`r pa_rng("S_inner_a0")` with categories 1 and 2 interchangeable
(@tbl-cfit-cal-adj). Compared with the rate before the correction, this keeps
`r rng(kept$share[kept$scale])` of the rejections for these three conditions
and `r rng(kept$share[!kept$scale])` for the weaker departures, in the cells
where the test rejected in more than 20% of datasets before the correction.
For example, step 2 discrimination 2 at n = 1000 and k = 10 went from
`r pw("S_inner_a2", 1000, 10)` to `r pa("S_inner_a2", 1000, 10)`. When the
focus item departed from the PCM, at least one of the other items was flagged
after the correction in at most `r pct(max(other_adj$rate))` of datasets per
cell.

```{r fig-cfit-cal-events}
#| label: fig-cfit-cal-events
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Rejection rate at .05 of the p for each cumulative event of the focus item at n = 1000 and k = 10, by condition. Dotted line at .05."
cal_ok |>
  filter(!null, n == 1000, k == 10) |>
  group_by(cond) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(paste0("p_raw_", 1:4)), ~ mean(.x < alpha)), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(paste0("p_raw_", 1:4)), names_to = "event", names_prefix = "p_raw_",
               values_to = "rate") |>
  mutate(event = paste0("X ≥ ", event)) |>
  ggplot(aes(event, rate, group = 1)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab(cond), ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Event", y = "Rejection rate") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 7.5))
```

The event that rejects points to the step concerned (@fig-cfit-cal-events).
Interchangeable categories 0 and 1 were found through $X \ge 1$, swapped or
interchangeable categories 1 and 2 and a step 2 that discriminated too much
or too little through $X \ge 2$, and "don't know" use in the middle category
through $X \ge 2$ and $X \ge 3$.

## Discussion {#sec-cfit-discussion}

The categories of an item can fail to work as scored while the threshold
estimates are ordered, and the estimates can be disordered while the PCM
fits. A test of the scoring therefore needs to compare the responses with
the model, not inspect the threshold order. `RMitemCatFit()` does this with
one p-value per item that held its level when the PCM was true, also with
disordered thresholds, and detected swapped and interchangeable categories
and steps that discriminate differently from the others. With its default
correction across items, the family-wise rate stayed close to .05.

`RMitemCatFitPlot()` shows where an item departs. The calibration plot points
to the step concerned, the residual and adjacent-category plots show which
categories are used by respondents with too low or too high scores, and the
rest-score plot shows the mean and spread of the rest score in each category, the most
sensitive view of "don't know" use.

Use and limits:

- **Iterations.** The default of 1000 simulated datasets took about a minute
  for 1000 respondents and eight items. With few iterations the p-values are
  coarse, and fewer than 400 give a notice.
- **"Don't know" use and response styles.** "Don't know" use in up to 10% of
  responses was rarely detected by any test, and a response style shared by
  all items is out of reach of a test that compares items. A mixture Rasch
  model or an IRTree model would be needed for the latter.
- **One departing item.** Only item 1 departed from the PCM in the study, and
  it was located at the centre of the person distribution. Departures in
  several items at once, and in items off target, were not studied.
- **Small samples.** At n = 250 some simulated datasets lose a category and
  cannot be refitted. The test then conditions on every category being
  observed, as it was in the observed data.
- **Pointwise bands.** The bands and intervals of `RMitemCatFitPlot()` are
  pointwise, a guide to where to look and not a test.

## Reproduction {#sec-cfit-reproduction}

The scripts are in `scripts/category-fit/` and are run from the book root.
They use their own implementation of the conditional probabilities and the
sampler (`functions.R`, `study_functions.R`, `calibration_functions.R`), with
psychotools for the CML estimates. The results the chapter reads are in
`results/category-fit/`. The per-cell files with one result per dataset are
not kept.

- **Per-category statistics.** `run_study.R`, 2 h 16 min on 10 cores.
  `summarise.R` writes `summary.rds`. The run computed the elementary
  symmetric functions by FFT convolution, and `functions.R` now uses direct
  polynomial multiplication, which is exact. In 60 datasets the difference
  moved $Q_j$ by at most 0.007 and the other statistics by at most 0.0001.
- **Calibration test.** `run_calibration_study.R`, about 6 h on 4 cores.
  `summarise_calibration.R` writes `calibration_summary.rds`, and
  `compare_combination.R` computes the item p-values and the correction
  across items from the stored simulated MCB values
  (`compare_combination.rds`, about 20 s).
- **Calibration test, B = 999.** `run_calibration_B999.R`, 81 min on 10
  cores. `summarise_calibration_B999.R` writes
  `calibration_b999_summary.rds`.

Seeds are fixed per cell, and the random-number streams depend on the number
of cores, so a run with another number of cores gives other datasets.

## Appendix: result tables {#sec-cfit-appendix}

```{r tbl-cfit-example}
#| label: tbl-cfit-example
#| tbl-cap: "RMitemCatFit() on the example data: p for each cumulative event, the item p and the item p corrected across items (Westfall-Young)."
fp <- easyRasch2:::.format_p_table
tb |>
  transmute(Item = item,
            `X ≥ 1` = fp(p_1), `X ≥ 2` = fp(p_2),
            `X ≥ 3` = fp(p_3), `X ≥ 4` = fp(p_4),
            `Item p` = fp(p), `Corrected p` = fp(padj)) |>
  kable()
```

```{r tbl-cfit-evaluable}
#| label: tbl-cfit-evaluable
#| tbl-cap: "Datasets per sample size and number of items in the study of the per-category statistics, all conditions together."
d |>
  group_by(Cell = cell) |>
  summarise(Datasets = n(),
            Skipped = sum(!is.na(skipped)),
            `No simulated dataset kept` = sum(is.na(skipped) & B_used == 0),
            `Kept < 90% of B` = sum(evaluable & B_used / B < .9),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  kable()
```

```{r tbl-cfit-thresholds}
#| label: tbl-cfit-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Mean CML threshold estimates of the focus item at n = 1000 and k = 10, and the rejection rate of the Wald test of threshold order."
ok |>
  filter(n == 1000, k == 10) |>
  group_by(Condition = lab(cond)) |>
  summarise(across(t1:t4, mean), `Wald, disorder` = mean(disorder_any)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r tbl-cfit-calibration}
#| label: tbl-cfit-calibration
#| tbl-cap: "Rejection rate at .05 for the focus item: calibration test (item p before the correction) and the p for each cumulative event, item index, and the Wald test of threshold order. The calibration test and the other two were run on different datasets."
cal_items |>
  filter(item == 1) |>
  group_by(cond, n, k) |>
  summarise(`Item p` = mean(p < alpha), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(cal_ok |>
              group_by(cond, n, k) |>
              summarise(`X ≥ 1` = mean(p_raw_1 < alpha), `X ≥ 2` = mean(p_raw_2 < alpha),
                        `X ≥ 3` = mean(p_raw_3 < alpha), `X ≥ 4` = mean(p_raw_4 < alpha),
                        .groups = "drop"),
            by = c("cond", "n", "k")) |>
  left_join(select(idx, cond, n, k, `Item index` = index, `Wald` = wald),
            by = c("cond", "n", "k")) |>
  mutate(Condition = lab(cond), Cell = sprintf("n = %d, k = %d", n, k)) |>
  arrange(Condition, k, n) |>
  select(Condition, Cell, `Item p`, starts_with("X"), `Item index`, Wald) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r tbl-cfit-cal-null}
#| label: tbl-cfit-cal-null
#| tbl-cap: "Calibration test when the PCM holds (B = 199): rejection rate of the item p over all items at .01 and .05, and the share of datasets with at least one item flagged after the Westfall-Young correction (family-wise rate)."
null_cell |>
  left_join(fwer, by = c("cond", "n", "k")) |>
  mutate(Condition = lab(cond), Cell = sprintf("n = %d, k = %d", n, k)) |>
  arrange(Condition, k, n) |>
  select(Condition, Cell, Datasets = datasets, `Item p < .01` = r01,
         `Item p < .05` = r05, `Family-wise rate` = fw) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r tbl-cfit-cal-adj}
#| label: tbl-cfit-cal-adj
#| tbl-cap: "Calibration test: rejection rate at .05 for the focus item before and after the Westfall-Young correction across items (B = 99), and the share of datasets with at least one of the other items flagged after the correction."
pow |>
  filter(test == "Calibration test") |>
  select(cond, n, k, Before = rate) |>
  left_join(rename(pow_adj, After = adj), by = c("cond", "n", "k")) |>
  left_join(rename(other_adj, `Other item flagged` = rate), by = c("cond", "n", "k")) |>
  mutate(Condition = lab(cond), Cell = sprintf("n = %d, k = %d", n, k)) |>
  arrange(Condition, k, n) |>
  select(Condition, Cell, Before, After, `Other item flagged`) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r tbl-cfit-cat-all}
#| results: asis
# Rejection rate at .05 per category of the focus item, every statistic and
# cell. Null cells have 500 datasets, the others 200.
for (st in names(pal_stat)) {
  tab <- rej |>
    filter(stat == st) |>
    mutate(Condition = lab(cond)) |>
    arrange(Condition, k, n) |>
    select(Condition, Cell = cell, category, rate) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = category, values_from = rate)
  print(kable(tab, digits = 2,
              caption = paste0("Rejection rate at .05 of the per-category statistic ",
                               st, " for categories 0 to 4 of the focus item.")))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```
